column4: Summary
In 1932 a researcher staying at the family's decaying estate wrote of his absent hosts and the strange noises he heard at night.
In July 1831 a cousin arrived in the dismal village to settle their late father's affairs and witnessed a grievous event.
The cold and dark landscape that dismayed their spouses only seemed to rejuvenate the young scientists.
The local paper took note of an ambitious inventor whose loud experiments revived old suspicions about the family.
Having already chosen a path towards destiny, a cousin basked in a brief affirmation of their own self-worth.
Unable to control their ambitious impulses, a cousin heard the townspeople whisper distrustfully as they walked by.
Pitchforks and torches gathered outside the gates, and only the hounds kept the mob from storming the estate.
Tired of angry mobs and frontier justice, a cousin had a grave plot installed upon the estate grounds.
In September 1850 the frightened crowd burned a suspected witch, and the cousins watched spellbound as the flames rose.
No suspicious eyes turned towards the family once the blaze died down, which proved fortunate for the cousins.
The Blacksmith laughed, shook each cousin's hand with a knowing wink and promised discounts with no questions asked.
Years later the village's paranoia had not faded, and the cousins knew their children would inherit the same suspicions.
A caretaker's letter warned the returning heirs that the village's hostility towards the family had flared up again.
A caretaker's letter told the returning heirs that the village's hostility towards the family had slowly softened.
Their caretaker confessed that the family's affairs held more secrets than one guardian could keep quiet.
Their caretaker reported that the village was returning to civility and the family's affairs were in order.
The second generation found their parents' obsessions boiling beneath their everyday activities.
The second generation struggled to resist the obsessions they had inherited from their parents.
Each cousin's private journal revealed the obsession that would drive their work for the generation.
Trusting only private couriers, a cousin wrote of the hexes and hysteria that had taken hold of the town.
Amid the gloom a movement grew to restore stability and celebrate what made Xvillage unique.
A messenger offered the least successful cousin a secret choice between fortune and misfortune.
After several business partners died, the townsfolk claimed the family carried a curse that brought tragedy to its allies.
To find the cursed cousin, the family took turns hexing a building in town and watched what befell it.
The paper reported hauntings in town, and everyone agreed that a curse lay upon Xvillage.
With charm and a little money, a cousin learned who had been seen hexing a building late one evening.
A courier delivered a package of unpublished scientific theories to a fortunate cousin's doorstep.
A servant was burned alive while tending the laundry, perhaps because of new laboratory security measures.

column2: Memorial to the Past for the Future
column4: The town's memorial lacked support, and the cousins were asked to decide whether to help build it.
The townspeople were grateful for the aristocracy's support while the caravans kept their distance.
A cousin wrote of the family tragedy in which the town demanded that one of them be accused of witchcraft.
The accusers pointed their fingers, and the cousin with the most accusations was chosen.
The accused cousin bravely faced death and was given a short reprieve to settle their final affairs.
The accused cousin barely escaped with their life and awaited judgement, certain that the town's jealousy knew no bounds.
In 1891 the mayor presented a solid gold Key to the City to the greatest contributor to the memorial.
The mayor announced a new monument whose design had been decided by public pressure and anonymous donations.
Years after the last fatal witchcraft accusation, the paper reported that no dark spirits had troubled the town since.
A brightly coloured caravan wagon opened as a market stall and brought colour to the grey town.
In March 1863 the horror of their grandfather's experiments returned to haunt the family.
The stitched-together Creature spoke of its hatred for its creator and made demands of his heirs.
The family realised that the plans passed down through the generations had produced a living monster.
Unwilling to let their grandfather's failure roam the countryside, a cousin resolved to perfect the family's technique.
The church accepted donations from cousins wishing to lower their creepy reputation.
Having created life only to feed a hideous fiend's urges, a cousin could not bear to look upon the finished experiment.
Behind its bleak exterior, the small asylum turned out to be clean and reasonably well run.
A cousin found a lost servant at the asylum, restrained but walking the grounds, diagnosed with extreme paranoia.
A cousin returned to the asylum, forgot they had already been there, and left with a sedative.
A cousin visited a gothic estate on the hill whose owner shared the family's tastes.
Over a sumptuous banquet the Count urged a cousin to donate to him instead of the asylum, with payment due in later years.
Praising a shrewd negotiator, the Count improved the terms of his offer.
The Count reddened at the refusal and had his man show the cousin out.
The Count shook hands on the contribution, and his touch sent an icy chill through the cousin.
Before the cousin left, the old Count softly asked for something that would take time to procure.
The new asylum opened with a ribbon-cutting ceremony attended by the mayor and the family.
A tall old man in black approached a cousin after the ceremony with a business proposal.
The asylum struggled financially and turned to private investors for support.
The asylum offered a new program to family members willing to make a generous donation.
The institution thanked the family, although the consequences of their decision would only become clear later.
The Creature returned to claim what it had asked for, threatening severe consequences.
A cousin made peace with the monster at the cost of their soul and freed their heirs from the family curse.
The donations to the asylum and to the Count were tallied, revealing where the family's support truly lay.
The enfeebled Count came to a cousin's door to ask for help with his ailment.
The Count accepted the prepared schematics and promised that his past mistakes would not be repeated.
Refused, the Count hissed like a feral cat and vanished in a burst of fog.
In 1892 men in dark overcoats interrupted a cousin's supper to collect what was owed to the Count.
Pleased with the payment, the Count's men left gracefully and pledged never to return.
The Count's men warned that their employer would not be pleased, and left in haste.
A worried correspondent asked why a cousin believed they had failed in the eyes of God by aiding the Creature.
Rumours spread that the asylum would become a private penitentiary, funded by the family's investments.
The Creature breached the estate at night and took its revenge on the family that had ignored its warnings.
The next morning the Creature left behind a bundle of old research notes, a small mercy amid the ruin.
Xenophobia took hold of the town, and those with conventional scientific aptitudes were met with distrust.
The town's push towards acceptance gave the cousins room to explore their obsessions.
Old tensions resurfaced and agitated the cousins' inherited obsessions.
A calmer town allowed the cousins a measure of peace from their obsessions.
Cousins who neglected their obsessions paid the price.
At a fork in the road outside town, a cousin arrived for a meeting and found no one waiting.
At the crossroads a cousin faced a long-delayed personal reckoning about the path their life had taken.
Refusing to give in to doubt, a cousin rededicated themselves to the work they had always desired.
Tired of being shackled to the family's destiny, a cousin chose to break free of it.
A note in elegant calligraphy appeared at a cousin's bedside: the debt had been repaid.
A brass key on a ruby silk pillow revealed that a cousin owned a second home in the region.
Pale figures in black suits got past the estate's defences, and a cousin hid under the stairs to write a final note.
The cloaked fiends took their payment and vanished in a flurry of bats against the full moon.
Refusing to pay, a cousin awaited certain death just as victory was within reach.
The cousins followed the Creature's trail through the snow-covered landscape.
The expedition revealed what had become of the Creature.
The cousins and their servants subdued and bound the Creature, ending its life.
The Creature bellowed into the valley under a pale moon and vanished once more into the mists.
In 1892 the townsfolk built a wall around their town, trading paranoia for delusion.
Grieving the death of a parent and distrusted by the townsfolk, a cousin withdrew into their study and dark research.
The people distrusted the cousins because of the deeds of their forebears, even in their birthplace.
On inspection day a cousin went to the shabby government offices to prove their citizenship.
In a cobwebbed Town Hall a cousin finally confirmed their own existence to the authorities.
The town demanded that every citizen verify their identity.
Another season passed without the Romani caravans, so the town held its own market instead.
A brazen warehouse proprietor offered a cousin smuggled goods over dinner.
The cousins agreed that the walled-in town made excellent controls for an experiment.
With little to invest in behind the walls, a cousin began a partnership with the local shipping company.
Accused of smuggling exotic goods on the roof of a carriage, a cousin was sentenced without trial.
A cousin was summoned to the courthouse, where the police would only present their evidence at trial.
Despite circumstantial evidence, the court could not make its smuggling case against the cousin.
The smuggling trial ended in a shameful display for the cousin.
A cousin admitted to smuggling goods from the docks and swore to do it again.
The cousins checked whether enough collaboration had gone into their creation.
In March 1912 a sudden implosion destroyed the Town Hall, killing four and injuring many.
An agitated gorilla injected with hormones and radium broke out of its cage.
The rampaging creation attacked the Bank after a soldier fired upon it.
The library collapsed into dust, books and blood as the creature paused, shaking violently.
The giant gorilla beat its chest one last time, and the rampage ended as quickly as it had begun.
A cousin raged that the others lacked the pioneering spirit to see the experiment through.
In April 1892 a cousin enjoyed no longer fearing being burned at the stake, though old habits remained.
Each place of business in town seemed to radiate the energy of a different faction.
Grateful for donations to the memorial, the local government reluctantly returned the favour.
The townsfolk felt a kinship with the family's suffering and pledged their service to a grieving cousin.
A celebrated cousin found that their fame inspired both their family and the town.
A strange tension hung in the air, warning of change on the horizon.
The factions were meant to tear each other apart at the town meeting, but the powder keg never exploded.
In June 1901 the townsfolk came to an agreement, and their tolerance brought the cousins some benefits.
On the brink of bloodshed, the townsfolk realised that they had one thing in common: they hated the family.
A cousin was haunted by nightmares of shambling crowds closing in.
The cousins voted on whether to steal the goods they needed under cover of darkness.
A cousin triumphed under cover of darkness and retrieved the goods they believed they deserved.
The cousins faltered under pressure and abandoned the plan to steal.
The cousin with the most occult experiments was awarded the Cabinet of Curiosities.
Another season passed without the Romani caravans, so the town held its own market instead.
In August 1892 a cousin wrote that the family now owned a substantial part of the town's commercial district.
The asylum had become a hastily built jail holding hundreds of wretches, deviants and criminals.
The parents' investments had matured, giving a cousin a substantial stake in the village.
The Count returned, apparently unaged, to offer the family investment opportunities.
The inmates took over the asylum in a chaotic rebellion and drove out its staff.
A cousin was forced to meet the leader of the rebellion on the steps of the prison.
The rebel leader admired the family's experiments and demanded that they build warriors.

column2: The World is Not the Same
column4: The cousins were tolerated only while useful, but gained the freedom to pursue any science they wished.
The rebel leader honoured the family's past support of the asylum with one exception.
The rebel leader demanded a sacrifice from the family.
Unable to procure fresh blood in the tainted village, the Count withdrew from his dealings.
Having burned every bridge with the scientific community, a cousin went to collect their hideous reward.
In the ruined mess hall the rebel leader praised a cousin for laying their soul bare.
A cousin ventured to the old jail at the centre of town to meet its new ruler.
Over a hideous outdoor feast, the rebel leader revealed a plan.

column2: The Meeting at the Junk Palace
column4: From a collapsed floor of the jail, the cousins looked out over the perverted land.
A cousin hurried away from the desolate palace, past a large figure lurking in the shadows.
A poorly written letter signed by The Creature showed that the family's old experiment was watching over them.
The rebel leader punished every cousin who had not reached the end of the Track.
The iron dome, draped in red cloth and hissing with steam, opened for the grand event.
An announcer on a penny-farthing presented the mechanical combatants to the crowd.
One warrior emerged from the pit of blood, oil and iron as champion, and the losers were swiftly punished.
In February 1892 a cousin found the town distressingly decent, cheerful and accepting.
The expanded asylum brought the town relative peace of mind.
A faded page listed the visitors and the patients admitted for psychiatric evaluation.
A case file recorded a cousin's troubling behaviour on admission.
Treatment concluded, and the patient was sent home with a care regimen.
After an informal interview, the patient was submitted to a formal psychological evaluation.
A full mental and physical examination produced the patient's assessment results.
Finding the asylum's methods timid, a cousin arranged to persuade its director to start an aggressive new program.
In 1902 the asylum unveiled a radical new treatment program in a wing full of complex machinery.
A vial of essential salts arrived, and a dead rabbit's heart began beating again: life from death.
Each cousin could try to use the salts to bring back their lost spouse.
A cousin broke into the mausoleum and applied the solution to their spouse's remains.
A cousin laid a lily on their spouse's grave, accepting that life is meant to end.
Recession and nationalist unrest left the family, as landowners, to decide how the regional government would proceed.
Parliament sharply rebuked the family's attempt to sway the democratic process.
A new income tax was introduced to reduce inequality across Transylvania.
The Nationalist movement in parliament prevailed.
The county levied an estate tax on wealthy citizens, interrupting a game of croquet.
Armed men arrived at the estates of the cousins who had avoided tax collection.
